newsitem.title: USA: US CREDIT MARKET OUTLOOK -- Short, quiet day seen.
newsitem.headline: US CREDIT MARKET OUTLOOK -- Short, quiet day seen.

text.p: The U.S. Treasuries market is expected to be as dead as the Thanksgiving turkey on Friday, with little or no movement in prices seen during an abbreviated session.
Typically, the Friday after Thanksgiving is the lightest trading day of the year, as most traders opt to take a long holiday weekend.
"It is a good day to take off because there are not a lot of people around," mused Terry Piggot, head trader at Daiwa Securities America Inc.
There could be a light flurry in the morning, as the Commerce Department releases October personal income and spending data at 0830 EST/1330 GMT, and the APICS survey is due at 1000 EST/1500 GMT.

The data "are old news so we are going to look ahead and turn the page to December," said William Sullivan, director of money markets research at Dean Witter Reynolds Inc. "Most likely, (the levels) where we finish today (Wednesday), we'll finish Friday."
Anlaysts noted that there could also be some minor month-end position squaring.

But for the most part, action should be very light. The market is scheduled to close at 1400 EST/1900 GMT, but traders said that the mostly skeleton staffs should be gone for the weekend long before that.

Piggot said much of the day will be spent watching CNN for anecdotal reports of holiday shopping. "Traders are anxious to see how sales are doing at the malls," he said. "They will watch for shopping bag counts."
How the season goes is crucial for the near term direction of the market, which hopes sales are weak enough to prompt the Federal Reserve to ease as its next move.

But given that most believe the Fed will next raise rates -- although the timing is unclear -- the short end of the market is stuck, leaving most action to the long end. The long bond is also expected to range near 6.40 percent.
Late Wednesday, the bond was at 100-29/32, up 6/32. Its yield edged down to 6.43 percent from 6.44 percent.

"The numbers (Wednesday) were stronger than expected, but there's still a whole group who still want to buy the market," Piggot said. "People are looking to buy on dips. Quite a bit has to change to get bearish."
